title: Reflecting Light
keyIdea: Light travels from a light source and bounces off the surfaces it hits. This bouncing is called reflection. Smooth, shiny surfaces such as a mirror, still water or a polished floor reflect light best: the light bounces off in one neat beam, so you can see a clear picture in them. Rough or dull surfaces like carpet, bark or paper send the light off in lots of directions, so there is no clear picture, and dark surfaces reflect very little. A mirror makes no light of its own: in the dark it shows nothing.
familyTip: In a dim room, shine a torch at a mirror and move the spot of light around the walls. Then try a spoon, a sheet of foil (flat, then crumpled), white paper and a dark jumper. Which gives a bright, neat spot? Next time it rains, look for a reflection in a puddle and blow on it to make ripples.

visual.caption: Could you see a clear reflection in it? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: bounce a torch beam onto a star, test six surfaces, switch the torch off, ripple a puddle and find reflections at home.

kid: Light comes from a light source, like the Sun, a lamp or a torch. When light hits something, it bounces off. We call this reflection.
Smooth, shiny things reflect light best. A mirror, a still pond and a polished floor send the light back in one neat beam. That is why you can see yourself in them.
Rough things, like carpet, bark or crumpled foil, send light off in lots of ways. You can not see a clear picture in them. Dark, dull things like black cloth hardly reflect any light.
A mirror does not make light. It only bounces light that falls on it. In a dark room, a mirror shows nothing. When wind makes ripples on a puddle, the water is bumpy, so its reflection breaks up.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. In England, Year 3 science asks children to notice that light is reflected from surfaces, and that we need light to see things. The NGSS also expects young children to test how light passes through or bounces off different materials (1-PS4-3). Key words: light, light source, reflect, reflection, surface, smooth, shiny, rough, dull, mirror.

Common mistakes: thinking shiny things such as a mirror, a spoon or the Moon make their own light; thinking light only reflects off mirrors (in fact most things reflect some light, which is how we see them, but rough ones scatter it); thinking light stops when it hits something; and thinking a crumpled piece of foil is as good as a flat one because both are shiny. Smooth matters as much as shiny.
The rule that light leaves a mirror at the same angle as it arrived comes later, in secondary school. Here the lab simply lets your child aim a torch so the bounced beam lands on a target.

In the lab your child aims a torch at a mirror to light up a star, tests six surfaces and compares how clear each bounce is, switches the torch off to see a mirror go dark, makes a puddle windy and calm, and finds the reflecting surfaces at home.

practice.prompt: What is it called when light bounces off a surface?
practice.hint: Think of the word for what a mirror does.
practice.explain: Light bouncing off a surface is called reflection. A mirror reflects light well.

practice.prompt: Jas tests {a} smooth, shiny things and {b} rough things with a torch. How many things does she test?
practice.hint: Add the shiny things and the rough things together.
practice.explain: {a} add {b} is {=a+b} things. Only the {a} smooth, shiny ones give a clear reflection.

practice.prompt: Which of these gives the clearest reflection?
practice.hint: Look for the smoothest, shiniest surface.
practice.explain: Still water is smooth and shiny, so it reflects light in one neat beam and you see a clear picture.

practice.prompt: A class finds {n} things that reflect a clear picture. {m} of them are mirrors. How many are not mirrors?
practice.hint: Take the mirrors away from all the things they found.
practice.explain: {n} take away {m} is {=n-m}. Things like spoons, polished floors and still water reflect clearly too.

practice.prompt: You switch off every light in a room with no windows. What do you see in the mirror?
choices: Nothing: there is no light to reflect
practice.hint: Does a mirror make light, or only bounce it?
practice.explain: A mirror makes no light. With no light to reflect, it shows nothing.

pool.prompt: Why can you see yourself in a mirror but not in a carpet?
choices: The mirror is smooth and shiny; the carpet is rough
The carpet is too far away
pool.hint: Think about how smooth each surface is.
pool.explain: A smooth, shiny mirror reflects light in one neat beam. Rough carpet sends light off in all directions.

pool.hint: A light source makes its own light, even in the dark.
pool.explain: A lit candle makes its own light. A mirror and a spoon only reflect light.

pool.prompt: You crumple a flat sheet of foil. What happens to its reflection?
choices: It breaks up: the bumps send light all over
pool.hint: Is crumpled foil smooth or bumpy?
pool.explain: Crumpled foil is still shiny, but its bumps send light in lots of directions. Smooth matters too.

pool.prompt: The wind blows across a pond. Why does the reflection of a tree go wobbly?
pool.hint: What does the wind do to the top of the water?
pool.explain: Ripples make the water bumpy, so the light bounces off in different ways and the picture breaks up.

pool.prompt: Light from a torch hits a mirror. What happens to the light?
pool.hint: Think about where the spot of light ends up.
pool.explain: The light bounces off the mirror. You can aim the bounced light at a wall.

pool.prompt: A torch spot moves {a} steps up a wall, then {b} steps down. How many steps up from the start is it now?
pool.hint: Start with {a} steps up and take away the {b} steps down.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b} steps up from where it began. Tilting the mirror moves the reflected spot.

pool.prompt: Which surface reflects the least light?
pool.hint: Dark, dull things send back very little light.
pool.explain: Black cloth is dark and dull, so hardly any light bounces back. That is why it looks dark.

pool.prompt: The Moon looks bright at night. Where does its light come from?
choices: The Moon makes its own light
pool.hint: Is the Moon a light source, or does it reflect light?
pool.explain: The Moon makes no light. It reflects light from the Sun back towards us.

pool.prompt: Sam's room has {k} mirrors with {s} shiny spoons, and {r} rough rugs. How many things in it give a clear reflection?
pool.hint: Count only the smooth, shiny things. Leave out the rugs.
pool.explain: {k} mirrors add {s} spoons is {=k+s}. The {r} rough rugs do not give a clear reflection.
